title: Standard Precautions and Waste Management in Healthcare
path: Control of Microorganisms and Infection Control
Standard Precautions and Waste Management in Healthcare

headings.title: Introduction to Infection Control in Nigerian Midwifery Practice
headings.content: Infection control is a daily responsibility for every midwife practicing in Nigeria. Midwives frequently manage vulnerable populations, including pregnant women, neonates, and postpartum mothers who face elevated risks of healthcare-associated infections. Microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, and fungi are present in all clinical environments, easily transmitted through blood, body fluids, non-intact skin, and mucous membranes. Implementing basic safety barriers disrupts the chain of transmission, protecting both patients and healthcare personnel from preventable illnesses like HIV, hepatitis B, and postpartum sepsis.

headings.title: Core Principles of Standard Precautions
headings.content: Standard precautions form the foundational level of infection control. They apply to every patient receiving care, regardless of their suspected or confirmed infection status. The core idea is simple: treat all blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes as if they are infectious. By assuming potential risk in every clinical interaction, midwives naturally build a habit of safety that prevents accidental exposure during routine procedures like vaginal examinations or catheter care.

headings.title: Proper Hand Hygiene and Personal Protective Equipment
headings.content:
Hand hygiene is widely recognized as the single most effective intervention for preventing the spread of healthcare-associated infections. Midwives must perform hand hygiene using soap and water when hands are visibly soiled, or an alcohol-based hand rub when hands are clean. Personal protective equipment (PPE) acts as a physical barrier between the midwife and infectious agents.

- **Gloves**: Wear when touching blood, body fluids, or mucous membranes; change between patients.
- **Aprons and Gowns**: Wear during procedures that are likely to generate splashes of blood or amniotic fluid.
- **Face Masks and Eye Protection**: Wear when managing deliveries or surgeries where body fluids may spray into the face.

headings.title: Safe Injection Practices and Sharps Injury Prevention
headings.content: Sharps injuries pose a severe occupational threat to midwives in Nigeria, exposing them to bloodborne viruses such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV. Safe injection practices protect both the healthcare provider and the parturient woman. Never recap needles using two hands. If recapping is unavoidable due to specific procedural constraints, use a single-handed scoop technique or a mechanical device. Immediately deposit used needles, syringes with attached needles, and scalpel blades into a puncture-resistant safety box located at the point of use.

headings.title: Comprehensive Waste Management in Healthcare Settings
headings.content: Healthcare activities generate diverse waste streams, ranging from harmless office paper to highly infectious anatomical parts and toxic chemicals. Poor waste management endangers clinical staff, cleaning personnel, waste handlers, and the surrounding community. A comprehensive waste management system requires clear policies, continuous staff training, adequate infrastructure, and strict adherence to segregation protocols right at the bedside. Treating all waste as general refuse creates immense environmental and public health hazards.

headings.title: Color-Coding and Segregation of Medical Waste
headings.content:
Effective waste segregation relies on standardized color-coding systems that allow instant identification of waste categories. Midwives must separate waste items immediately as they are generated, rather than sorting them later.

| Waste Category | Standard Color Coding | Typical Midwifery Examples |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| General / Non-Hazardous | Black or Transparent | Food wrappers, office paper, carton boxes |
| Infectious Waste | Yellow | Soiled cotton balls, placenta, gauze, gloves |
| Sharps Waste | Yellow with puncture-proof lid | Needles, scalpels, suture needles, ampoules |
| Chemical / Pharmaceutical | Brown | Expired oxytocin, leftover disinfectants |

headings.title: Safe Disposal and Transport of Hazardous Materials
headings.content: Once waste is safely segregated, its journey does not end at the ward door. Hazardous waste requires specialized treatment methods such as high-temperature incineration, autoclaving, or chemical disinfection before final burial. Transporting waste within the health facility must be done using leak-proof, covered trolleys or bins that are never overfilled. Staff responsible for moving waste bags must wear heavy-duty utility gloves, aprons, and boots to protect against accidental spills, punctures, or chemical splashes.

headings.title: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis and Incident Reporting
headings.content: Despite rigorous precautions, accidental needle-stick injuries and body fluid splashes still occur in clinical practice. When an exposure incident happens, a midwife must act calmly and promptly. First, encourage bleeding under running water for puncture wounds—do not scrub or suck the wound. Wash affected skin with soap and water, and rinse splashes to the eyes or mouth with copious clean water. Report the incident immediately to the facility's infection control officer or supervisor to evaluate the source patient's infection status and initiate timely Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) when indicated.
